title: Persistent Web Skills Runtime
pitch: A WebMCP-first runtime that learns browser workflows once, reuses them reliably, and repairs them when the web changes.
about_excerpt: A WebMCP-first runtime that learns browser workflows once, reuses them reliably, and repairs them when the web changes. Like Comment Story Updates Persistent Web Skills Runtime Persistent Web Skills Runtime (PWS) is a WebMCP-first Chrome runtime that lets agents learn a browser workflow once, reuse it as a versioned skill, and repair it when the web changes. The problem Agentic browser tasks are commonly rediscovered through fragile clicks on every run. Small UI changes can break a workflow, while useful structured WebMCP tools may be ignored or forgotten. Repeated exploration is slow, brittle, token-intensive, and hard to trust. The solution PWS routes each task through a clear priority ladder: Native WebMCP → Cached Web Skill → Browser/DOM learning fallback It discovers the page's current WebMCP tools first. If there is no suitable native tool, it learns a successful semantic browser workflow, stores it in IndexedDB with immutable version history, validates the outcome on reuse, and repairs only the failed step when a dependency changes. The live taskboard demo shows an 11-action Learn → Reuse → Repair flow: it learns a create-task workflow, reuses it, survives a Create Task → Add Task UI change with a validated v1 → v2 skill repair, and demonstrates live native tool registration through toolchange . Key features Native-first WebMCP routing via document.modelContext.getTools() , live toolchange synchronization, and current-tool rebinding. Safe capability snapshots that persist metadata, not executable tool handlers. Semantic locators based on role, name, labels, stable attributes, and meaningful text instead of brittle structural selectors. Dependency-only DOM fingerprints, explicit result validation, and targeted step repair. An inspectable Runtime Inspector, execution log, timings, validation status, and skill versions. Built with React, TypeScript, Vite, a Chrome Manifest V3 extension, IndexedDB, Node.js, and an optional OpenAI Responses API service. API keys remain server-side; the interactive demo runs without a key through deterministic local learning and repair adapters. Career value I work as an agent engineer and repeatedly test browser automation over many fresh pages. I wanted a way for agents to achieve stronger results with fewer tokens. Building PWS made the practical value of WebMCP clear: expose structured tools, preserve proven workflows as reusable skills, and give agents a safe answer to reuse instead of forcing them to rediscover the UI. This can make agent browser work faster, more reliable, and easier to trust.
